verdicts.stack: WinUI 3 / Windows App SDK 2.0 (C#/.NET 10, WinRT, Microsoft.UI.Composition, Win2D + ComputeSharp.D2D1)
verdicts.verdict: DISQUALIFIED - the stack's two halves are mutually exclusive: the only API that samples desktop content behind the window (SystemBackdrop / DesktopAcrylicController) is a closed system material with four tint knobs and no pixel access, while the only API that runs a custom fragment shader (Win2D/D2D1 PixelShaderEffect) can only consume images the app itself owns, and Microsoft's own docs mark PixelShaderEffect [NoComposition] so the two cannot be bridged.
verdicts.glass: Blur and tint only, no lensing. Honest answer in three parts. (1) DESKTOP AS A TEXTURE: no. Microsoft.UI.Composition.Compositor - the lifted compositor WinUI 3 actually uses - exposes CreateBackdropBrush() and has NO CreateHostBackdropBrush() at all in its method list through Windows App SDK 2.0; CreateBackdropBrush samples only what is behind the visual inside the app's own composition tree. The UWP-only Windows.UI.Composition.Compositor.CreateHostBackdropBrush() does sample behind the window, but its own Remarks state flatly "The app cannot read the pixel data back," it is already blurred and translucent before you get it, and "The transparency of the host backdrop brush is a property the user can control from Settings or by using power policies." The WinUI 3 route is Window.SystemBackdrop = DesktopAcrylicBackdrop (or MicaBackdrop / SystemBackdropElement in WinAppSDK 2.0), and Microsoft's in-app-acrylic page states outright that "The UWP BackgroundSource property (which enabled a HostBackdrop mode for window-level acrylic) is not available in WinUI 3." DesktopAcrylicController exposes exactly four customisable properties - TintColor, TintOpacity, LuminosityOpacity, FallbackColor - plus a Base/Thin Kind enum. That is a fixed DWM material, not a backdrop you can process. (2) CUSTOM FRAGMENT SHADER OVER THAT BACKDROP: no. The composition effect library is a closed list of 14 effect types (affine transform, arithmetic composite, blend, color source, composite, contrast, exposure, grayscale, gamma transfer, hue rotate, invert, saturate, sepia, temperature/tint); the docs say "Effects not supported in composition are noted as [NoComposition]" and Win2D's PixelShaderEffect reference says explicitly "Supported by Win2D but not Windows.UI.Composition" and carries the [NoComposition] attribute. Custom shaders ARE reachable on this stack - Win2D PixelShaderEffect, or ComputeSharp.D2D1.WinUI's PixelShaderEffect<T> which lets you write D2D1 pixel shaders in C# with build-time HLSL transpilation, and with SamplerCoordinateMapping.Offset + MaxSamplerOffset they can sample away from the current pixel, so genuine lensing, refraction and a specular rim ARE expressible, and so is the Genie.metal distortion. But the shader's inputs must be ICanvasImage - bitmaps, render targets, other Win2D effects. A CompositionBackdropBrush is a CompositionBrush and cannot be handed to a Win2D drawing session. There is no API that converts the backdrop into a texture. This is the wall. (3) POINTER-TRACKING .interactive(): yes, trivially, for whichever of the two paths you pick - composition effect properties are animatable per-frame via CompositionPropertySet / ExpressionAnimation, and a ComputeSharp shader's constant buffer is rewritten per draw on a CanvasAnimatedControl. Pointer response is the easy part and it does not rescue the rest. NET RESULT AGAINST THE FIELD EVIDENCE: the port can have lensing over app-drawn content (the Wallpaper.swift layer, re-expressed as a Win2D surface) OR blur-and-tint over the desktop, never lensing over the desktop. The observed edge refraction with chromatic fringing where the window border crosses high-contrast desktop content is not reproducible. This is confirmed independently by the most serious community attempt, LiquidGlassWinUI3, whose pipeline is "DWM HostBackdrop -> CompositionBackdropBrush -> per-surface GaussianBlurEffect -> rounded clip -> tint, rim highlight, inner/outer shadow, pointer response" and whose README concedes that for RefractionAmount and ChromaticAberration "the current backend retains depth styling but does not apply those two sampling effects," and that "HostBackdrop and desktop pixels are not read into application memory." The only remaining path to desktop pixels is Windows.Graphics.Capture, which is not a material API: it needs GraphicsCaptureAccess.RequestAccessAsync with GraphicsCaptureAccessKind.Borderless plus the graphicsCaptureWithoutBorder manifest capability merely to suppress the yellow recording border, shows the user a consent prompt, would require SetWindowDisplayAffinity(WDA_EXCLUDEFROMCAPTURE) on our own window to avoid feedback (which then blanks the app in the user's own screenshots and screen shares), and delivers a frame-late full-screen texture every frame. Under OD-0003 that is not a fidelity solution, it is a liability.

verdicts.stack: Native Win32 + Direct3D 11/12 + Direct2D + DirectComposition (C++), with DirectWrite for text, HLSL for the material shaders, Windows.Graphics.Capture for desktop backdrop sampling, and ConPTY for the terminal.
verdicts.verdict: VIABLE - it is, on the evidence I could find, the only candidate class that can actually obtain desktop pixels as a shadable texture and run arbitrary HLSL over them, so it clears OD-0003; but it clears it by paying a documented capture tax (self-exclusion from all screen capture, a consent/border gate, and one-to-two frames of backdrop lag) and it carries by far the highest build cost, because every control, the UI Automation tree, IME, and the terminal emulator are hand-built.
verdicts.glass:
It can do real lensing, not just blur and tint - but not through any backdrop API. The honest breakdown:

(a) DESKTOP CONTENT AS A TEXTURE: YES, but only via screen capture, never via a backdrop brush. Every backdrop-shaped API on Windows is closed. DWM's system backdrop is a fixed enum with five values (DWMSBT_AUTO/NONE/MAINWINDOW/TRANSIENTWINDOW/TABBEDWINDOW); DWMSBT_TRANSIENTWINDOW is documented as "Desktop Acrylic ... in its brightest variant" and there is no parameter to alter it and no way to read its pixels. Windows.UI.Composition's Compositor.CreateHostBackdropBrush does "sample from the area behind the visual, before the window is drawn" - which is exactly the macOS semantic - but the Remarks state flatly: "The app cannot read the pixel data back." It is a brush you may only feed into WinComp's fixed effect graph. So the DWM/WinComp route is blur-and-tint only.

The route that does work is Windows.Graphics.Capture. From a Win32 desktop app, IGraphicsCaptureItemInterop::CreateForMonitor (windows.graphics.capture.interop.h, Win10 1903+) creates a GraphicsCaptureItem for the monitor with no GraphicsCapturePicker. Direct3D11CaptureFramePool.Create + CreateCaptureSession + StartCapture then delivers Direct3D11CaptureFrame objects whose Surface is an ID3D11Texture2D on your own D3D device. That is real desktop pixels in a shader resource view. To stop the window mirroring itself into its own backdrop, the app calls SetWindowDisplayAffinity(hwnd, WDA_EXCLUDEFROMCAPTURE) (0x11, Windows 10 2004+), after which "the window does not appear at all" in the capture - which yields exactly the content behind the window.

(b) ARBITRARY FRAGMENT SHADER OVER THAT BACKDROP: YES, unconditionally. Once the desktop is an ID3D11Texture2D you are in your own D3D11 pipeline with your own HLSL. Refraction/lensing is a sample-coordinate remap; chromatic fringing is three offset samples of R, G and B at different refraction strengths; the specular edge is a signed-distance-field rim term over the shape. Nothing about this is gated. The window itself is a DXGI composition swap chain (IDXGIFactory2::CreateSwapChainForComposition, which supports only the flip model) bound as content of an IDCompositionVisual via IDCompositionVisual::SetContent, on a WS_EX_NOREDIRECTIONBITMAP window, so DWM composites your per-pixel-alpha output over the desktop. The Genie.metal shader at UI/Common/Genie.metal is a pure float2 position remap with no Metal-specific features; it is a near-literal transliteration to an HLSL pixel shader.

(c) PER-FRAME POINTER RESPONSE FOR .interactive(): YES, and this is the easiest of the three. You own the frame loop and the constant buffer. Pointer position from WM_MOUSEMOVE (or WM_POINTERUPDATE) goes into a cbuffer each frame; the shader deforms around it. There is no framework between you and the draw call.

THE HONEST COSTS, which are product costs, not capability costs:
1. WDA_EXCLUDEFROMCAPTURE makes the app invisible to the user's OWN screenshots, Snipping Tool, OBS, and Teams/Zoom screen shares. For a coding-agent tool whose users screenshot transcripts and share screens in reviews, that is a severe regression the macOS original does not have. The alternative - not excluding - is an infinite-mirror feedback loop.
2. GraphicsCaptureSession.IsBorderRequired = false is ignored unless the process first calls GraphicsCaptureAccess.RequestAccessAsync(GraphicsCaptureAccessKind.Borderless), and the docs say that "displays a prompt to the user" and requires declaring the graphicsCaptureWithoutBorder capability "in your app's package manifest." Without it, Windows 11 draws a yellow recording border around the ENTIRE MONITOR for as long as the app is open. Field reports claim unpackaged desktop processes are granted this silently on Win11 Pro, but that is not in the official documentation - see probe 1.
3. Capture frames arrive asynchronously via FrameArrived. The lensed region will be one to two frames behind the true desktop, while any genuinely transparent (alpha-blended, unblurred) region of the same window is exact. During a window drag those two disagree visibly. macOS has no such seam because the compositor does the sampling in-band.
4. Glass over the app's OWN wallpaper layer (UI/Theme/Wallpaper.swift) needs none of this: render app content to an offscreen RTV and shade it. That subset is full fidelity with zero caveats. Only the over-desktop subset pays the tax.
5. Even with total pixel control, macOS 26 Liquid Glass is an unpublished algorithm. PA-0001 already records that the source contains no pre-Liquid-Glass fallback, so the look must be converged on empirically from side-by-side captures. Native D3D is the only stack class where that iteration is even possible, but it is still reverse-engineering, not transliteration.

verdicts.stack: Avalonia UI 12.1.2 (current stable, Sept 2026) on .NET 10, rendering through SkiaSharp 4.152.x / Skia, with HarfBuzzSharp shaping, the Avalonia composition renderer, and Win32/WinRT interop via Win32Properties and MicroCom.
verdicts.verdict: UNRESOLVED - pending an owner ruling on OD-0003, not on a technical fact. Avalonia can render a genuine custom Liquid Glass material with per-pixel lensing, specular edge and pointer-tracked deformation over content the APP draws, but it cannot do so over the DESKTOP, and neither can any other Windows stack, because Windows exposes no readable backdrop texture; on the literal wording of OD-0003 ("the exact same look... zero guesswork", with field evidence of edge refraction and chromatic fringing over desktop widgets) the default window configuration FAILS, and that failure is a platform ceiling rather than an Avalonia property, so ruling Avalonia DISQUALIFIED would disqualify every candidate identically.
verdicts.glass:
Answered in three parts, because the honest answer differs by what sits behind the glass.

(1) DESKTOP behind the window, as a texture Avalonia can shade: NO. Avalonia's `WindowTransparencyLevel.AcrylicBlur` is implemented in `Avalonia.Win32/WindowImpl.cs` via `SetTransparencyAcrylicBlur()`, which sets `DWMWA_USE_HOSTBACKDROPBRUSH` and calls `CompositionEffectsSurface.SetBlur(BlurEffect.Acrylic)`; that resolves to `WinUiCompositionUtils.CreateAcrylicBlurBackdropBrush`, whose source is `ICompositor3::CreateHostBackdropBrush()`. Microsoft's reference for that method states plainly: "The host backdrop brush tells the compositor to sample from the area behind the visual, before the window is drawn... The app cannot read the pixel data back." The sampled desktop lives in a DirectComposition sprite visual BEHIND Avalonia's Skia surface. Skia never sees those pixels. So the desktop is available as a system-composited layer, never as a texture.

(2) Custom fragment shader over that backdrop: NO. Even inside the composition graph, `Compositor.CreateEffectFactory` documents a closed list of six supported effect types - ArithmeticCompositeEffect, CompositeEffect, BlendEffect (21 of 26 modes), ColorSourceEffect, SaturationEffect, Transform2DEffect. There is no DisplacementMapEffect, no custom pixel shader, no D2D custom effect registration. Blur radius, tint, saturation and an affine transform are all that is expressible. That yields blur-and-tint, and at most a uniform affine magnification - it cannot produce edge-concentrated refraction falloff, per-channel chromatic fringing, or a specular highlight derived from backdrop luminance. Blur-and-tint only, no lensing, is the accurate description of the desktop-backdrop path.

(3) App-drawn content behind the glass: YES, fully. `ISkiaSharpApiLease` (src/Skia/Avalonia.Skia/ISkiaSharpApiLeaseFeature.cs) exposes `SKCanvas SkCanvas`, `GRContext? GrContext` and `SKSurface? SkSurface`. `SkSurface.Snapshot()` gives an `SKImage` of everything drawn beneath the glass site in the same frame; that image becomes a child shader uniform to an `SKRuntimeEffect` compiled from SKSL. From there refraction, edge-concentrated displacement, per-channel offsets for fringing, adaptive tinting sampled from backdrop luminance and a specular rim are all ordinary shader work. The official Avalonia blog post "Avalonia with Fragment Shaders" documents exactly this pipeline: `SKRuntimeEffect.Create`, `SKRuntimeEffectUniforms`, a `CompositionCustomVisualHandler.OnRender(ImmediateDrawingContext)` taking `ISkiaSharpApiLeaseFeature`, and per-frame animation via `RegisterForNextAnimationFrameUpdate()` / `OnAnimationFrameUpdate()` with `CompositionNow.TotalSeconds`.

(4) Per-frame pointer response for `.interactive()`: YES, on the same path as (3). The pointer position is just another uniform pushed each animation frame. This is unconstrained.

The bite: the source makes the desktop case the DEFAULT, not an edge case. `UI/Theme/Wallpaper.swift` / `WindowBackdrop` shows the no-wallpaper branch is `shape.fill(.clear).glassEffect(in: shape)` with only a scrim (0.26 dark / 0.18 light) - bare glass over the desktop - and the wallpaper branch paints the picture at the slider's own opacity so the desktop still shows through. Because the window backdrop is itself transparent, the other 18 inner glass sites stack over a surface that is transparent to the desktop, so they inherit the same limit. Only at backdrop opacity >= 0.98 (the `isSolid` branch, which deliberately drops glass for a plain fill) or a fully opaque wallpaper does the app own its own backdrop, and there path (3) delivers full fidelity.

One escape hatch exists and is not Avalonia-specific: capture the desktop yourself as a D3D11 texture. `IDXGIOutputDuplication` (DXGI Desktop Duplication) or `IGraphicsCaptureItemInterop::CreateForMonitor` (Windows.Graphics.Capture) both give real desktop pixels; `SetWindowDisplayAffinity(hwnd, WDA_EXCLUDEFROMCAPTURE)` (Win10 2004+) keeps the app's own window out of the capture and so breaks the feedback loop. That texture could then be bound as an SKSL child shader and path (3) would apply to the desktop too. The costs are severe and must be stated: the app becomes permanently invisible in the user's own screen shares and recordings (WDA_EXCLUDEFROMCAPTURE covers BitBlt, DDA, WGC and DWM thumbnails alike - a coding-agent tool that cannot be demoed or screen-shared is a real product regression); the Windows.Graphics.Capture variant additionally draws a coloured capture border around the whole display unless `GraphicsCaptureSession.IsBorderRequired = false`, which Microsoft documents requires user consent via `GraphicsCaptureAccess.RequestAccessAsync(GraphicsCaptureAccessKind.Borderless)` AND the `graphicsCaptureWithoutBorder` capability declared in a package manifest - i.e. MSIX packaging, which an unpackaged installer does not have; the glass lags the desktop beneath it by at least one composition frame, visibly smearing while the window is dragged; and the D3D11-texture-into-Skia interop (ANGLE `EGL_ANGLE_d3d_texture_client_buffer`, or the Vulkan backend with external memory) is unproven in Avalonia and is the single largest unknown in this whole assessment.

verdicts.stack: Qt 6.11 (current shipping release; docs served as 6.11.1/6.11.2), C++ with QML/Qt Quick on the RHI scene graph, Direct3D 11 backend on Windows, plus direct Win32/DXGI calls for anything Qt does not wrap.
verdicts.verdict: VIABLE (conditional) - Qt 6 can render the material itself (arbitrary baked fragment shaders over an arbitrary texture, per-frame uniforms, transparent DirectComposition-backed window), so it is not disqualified by OD-0003; but the desktop backdrop must be acquired by the app itself through DXGI Desktop Duplication or Windows.Graphics.Capture, because no Windows compositor API hands any stack the pixels behind its window, and two properties of that self-capture path are unproven on this machine.
verdicts.glass:
Split the question, because the two halves have different answers.

(a) Can Qt obtain the DESKTOP content behind its own window as a texture? Not through any Qt API and not through any Windows compositor API. Windows' only "sample what is behind the window" primitive is Compositor.CreateHostBackdropBrush, and its documented remark is explicit: "The host backdrop brush tells the compositor to sample from the area behind the visual, before the window is drawn... The app cannot read the pixel data back." It is also not programmable - a CompositionBrush effect graph is a fixed Win2D-style effect set, not HLSL, and DWMWA_SYSTEMBACKDROP_TYPE (Mica / Acrylic / Tabbed) is composited by DWM entirely outside the app's render graph. So the system route is blur-and-tint only, with no lensing, and it is the same dead end for Electron, Tauri, WinUI, Avalonia and Qt alike. Under OD-0003 that route alone is a fail.

The only way any Windows process gets those pixels as a sampleable texture is to capture the screen itself: IDXGIOutputDuplication::AcquireNextFrame (Desktop Duplication API) returns the composed desktop as a DXGI_FORMAT_B8G8R8A8_UNORM surface that QIs straight to ID3D11Texture2D, in-process, with no picker and no capture border; or Windows.Graphics.Capture via IGraphicsCaptureItemInterop::CreateForMonitor, which also skips the picker but draws the yellow capture border unless the app declares the restricted graphicsCaptureWithoutBorder capability in a package manifest and the user consents to GraphicsCaptureAccessKind.Borderless - which forces MSIX identity and collides with constraint 11. So Desktop Duplication is the route, and the app's own window must be taken out of the capture (SetWindowDisplayAffinity WDA_EXCLUDEFROMCAPTURE, Windows 10 2004+) or the glass will feed back on itself.

(b) Given that texture, can Qt run a custom fragment shader over it to produce lensing, refraction and a specular edge rather than only blur and tint? Yes, unambiguously. Qt 6's shader pipeline compiles GLSL 440 to SPIR-V and translates it to HLSL for Direct3D 11, packed into .qsb files consumed by ShaderEffect or a QSGMaterialShader. Arbitrary sampling offsets, chromatic separation per channel, edge-distance specular terms and signed-distance shape masks are ordinary fragment-shader work, so the Genie .distortionEffect shader is also a direct transliteration (Metal to GLSL, then qsb).

(c) Can it respond per frame to pointer position for .interactive()? Yes - a ShaderEffect property bound to a MouseArea/HoverHandler position becomes a shader uniform updated every frame with no special machinery.

Honest summary: Qt is not the limiting factor for the material; Windows is the limiting factor for the backdrop. Qt is fully capable of the specular-edge, refracting, pointer-deforming material, and for the glass that sits over the app's own wallpaper layer (UI/Theme/Wallpaper.swift) it can do it at full fidelity with no OS involvement at all, via ShaderEffectSource / layer.effect over the app's own scene. For the glass that sits over the DESKTOP, fidelity depends on a self-capture backdrop that is one composited frame stale, includes windows stacked ABOVE the app (macOS samples only what is behind), and makes the app invisible to screen sharing and screenshots if WDA_EXCLUDEFROMCAPTURE is used. That last consequence is a product-level cost for a coding-agent app people screen-share, and it applies to every Windows stack equally.

verdicts.stack: Electron 44.x (Chromium + Node), TypeScript, with node-pty/xterm.js, electron-builder NSIS + electron-updater
verdicts.verdict: VIABLE - not disqualified under OD-0003, because Chromium can genuinely refract a live backdrop (empirically confirmed here, not inferred), but it is viable only if the port accepts a self-built capture-and-redraw compositor for the one window-sized glass surface that sits over the desktop, and accepts that the app's primary visual identity then rests on a documented non-interoperable Chromium behaviour plus a continuous screen-capture stream.
verdicts.glass:
It is NOT "blur and tint only", and I can show that rather than assert it. Three separate questions, three different answers.

(1) DESKTOP CONTENT BEHIND THE WINDOW AS A TEXTURE - not through any compositing API. Electron's own docs are explicit: "The CSS blur() filter only applies to the window's web contents, so there is no way to apply blur effect to the content below the window (i.e. other applications open on the user's system)." The CSS spec agrees structurally: backdrop-filter reads the Backdrop Root Image, "the final image produced by painting all content in painting order between (and including) the ancestor Backdrop Root element and element E" - document content only. win.setBackgroundMaterial('acrylic') does get Desktop Acrylic, which per Microsoft "reveals the desktop wallpaper and other windows that are behind the currently active app", but DWM draws it BEHIND the window; the app cannot read it back, shade it, or displace it. Its recipe is fixed ("background, blur, exclusion blend, color/tint overlay, noise") and customizable only in tint colour and opacity. Worse for this app: it "appears as a solid color ... when the user turns off Transparency effects", in Battery Saver, on low-end hardware, and "when an app window on desktop deactivates" - i.e. the whole surface flattens to a solid fill every time the window loses focus, which is precisely the failure contract section 10 forbids. Acrylic is therefore not merely insufficient, it is actively disqualifying as the window-level material.
The ONLY path to desktop pixels is screen capture: desktopCapturer plus ses.setDisplayMediaRequestHandler, which can grant a screen source programmatically with no picker ("callback({ video: sources[0] })"), producing a MediaStreamTrack you upload to a WebGL/WebGPU texture each frame. Self-capture feedback is solvable: win.setContentProtection(true) "calls SetWindowDisplayAffinity with WDA_EXCLUDEFROMCAPTURE. For Windows 10 version 2004 and up the window will be removed from capture entirely" - at the permanent cost that the user can never screenshot or screen-share the app.

(2) CUSTOM FRAGMENT SHADER PRODUCING LENSING AND A SPECULAR EDGE - yes, by two independent mechanisms, and I probed both in Chromium 152 on Windows.
(a) backdrop-filter WITH an SVG reference filter actually displaces the live backdrop. I rendered two identical rounded panels over a high-contrast diagonal stripe field; the panel with backdrop-filter: url(#disp) blur(6px) showed the stripes genuinely warped and torn by the feDisplacementMap, the panel with blur(6px) alone showed flat blur. CSS.supports('backdrop-filter','url(#disp)') returned true and the computed value retained url("#disp") blur(6px). This is real refraction of content behind the element and it covers 21 of the 22 glass sites - every in-window surface sitting over app-drawn content. Caveat stated plainly: this is NOT interoperable. WebKit bug 245510 reports it does not work there, and w3c/svgwg#1142 exists because the platform "lacks a reliable way to apply this kind of displacement to the live backdrop behind an element". Electron ships one pinned engine, so single-engine behaviour is usable - but the app's entire visual identity would then depend on unspecified Blink behaviour, making the Electron pin load-bearing.
(b) WebGL2 and WebGPU are both present (navigator.gpu present, WebGL 2.0 via ANGLE/D3D11). I wrote and ran a fragment shader that does the full recipe in one pass: signed-distance-field rounded rect, gradient-driven edge refraction that visibly bends the background stripes at the border, a specular rim highlight, a multi-tap blur, adaptive tint, and an exponential pointer-tracked deformation term. It rendered correctly. This is also the natural home for Genie.metal - a Metal fragment shader reached through .distortionEffect transliterates to GLSL/WGSL almost line for line, which makes it the single lowest-translation constraint in the whole set.

(3) PER-FRAME POINTER RESPONSE for .interactive() - mechanically yes; both routes take per-frame input (a shader uniform, or rewriting feDisplacementMap/feImage attributes per pointermove). Whether it sustains 60 fps at 1320x860 on the target AMD integrated GPU is UNRESOLVED and I will not claim it. My timing runs are invalid and I am discarding them rather than reporting them: the embedded pane throttled requestAnimationFrame to near zero when not actively painted, and it reported an NVIDIA RTX 4080 via ANGLE/D3D11, not the AMD integrated GPU in the brief - so it is not the target machine and its compositor is not the target compositor. Worth flagging separately: that GPU mismatch suggests the machine inventory in the brief should be re-verified before any stack decision leans on it. One structural observation from the runs does survive and matters: Chromium caches the backdrop-filter result and only recomputes on invalidation (a static full-window filtered panel free-ran while a per-frame-animated one did not). That is exactly the cost model Chrome.swift:219 warns about - .interactive() plus a live streaming transcript invalidates continuously, so the window-sized surface really is a full-window resample every frame.

BOTTOM LINE: backdrop sampling YES (of DOM content natively; of the desktop only via screen capture), blur YES, specular edge YES, lensing/refraction YES, pointer deformation YES. Not disqualified. The honest asterisk is that the desktop-facing half requires the port to build its own compositor out of a capture stream, which no compositing API in this stack provides.

verdicts.stack: Tauri 2 (Rust core + wry/WebView2 on Windows), with window-vibrancy 0.8 for window effects
verdicts.verdict: DISQUALIFIED - the web content in a Tauri window can never obtain desktop pixels as a sampleable backdrop, so the glass that the field captures show (window nearly transparent over the desktop wallpaper, with edge refraction and chromatic fringing over desktop content) reduces to DWM Acrylic/Mica blur-and-tint, which OD-0003 and PA-0001 explicitly reject.
verdicts.glass:
Split answer, and the half that matters fails.

DESKTOP-BACKED GLASS: FAIL, structurally, not as a bug. A Chromium page's backdrop for `backdrop-filter` is defined as the painted content of the Backdrop Root, i.e. content inside the document; nothing outside the web document (the OS desktop behind a transparent window) is ever part of it (W3C Filter Effects 2 / the Chromium backdrop-filter explainer: "all of the painted content that lies behind the element ... almost everything behind the page"). The w3c/svgwg issue on liquid-glass refraction states the position plainly: Apple does this in the OS compositor, and the web platform has no equivalent over content it does not paint. So the only desktop-behind effect available to a Tauri window is the system one: window-vibrancy 0.8 `apply_blur` / `apply_acrylic` / `apply_mica` / `apply_tabbed`, which are thin wrappers over the undocumented `user32.dll!SetWindowCompositionAttribute` with `ACCENT_ENABLE_BLURBEHIND` / `ACCENT_ENABLE_ACRYLICBLURBEHIND`, and `DwmSetWindowAttribute(DWMWA_SYSTEMBACKDROP_TYPE, DWMSBT_MAINWINDOW | DWMSBT_TRANSIENTWINDOW | DWMSBT_TABBEDWINDOW)` (verified by reading window-vibrancy/src/windows.rs at dev). Those take a tint colour and nothing else: no shader hook, no per-pixel control, no lensing, no specular edge, no pointer input. Blur and tint only. That is exactly the substitution PA-0001 calls "one step less flat" than the flattening contract section 10 forbids.

APP-DRAWN-CONTENT GLASS: genuinely better than I expected, and it does not rescue the verdict. Chromium (and therefore WebView2) is the one engine that honours `backdrop-filter: url(#svgFilter)`, so an `feDisplacementMap` fed by a Snell's-law displacement map over the live DOM backdrop gives real lensing, per-channel displacement gives chromatic fringing, and an `feBlend`ed rim pass gives the specular edge. Safari and Firefox drop the SVG part; Chromium runs it. Pointer tracking is achievable by animating filter parameters (`scale`) per `pointermove`, though the published work says any shape or size change "forces a full displacement map rebuild", and the map is capped at 127 samples per radius. The Genie `.distortionEffect` shader has the same route: an SVG `feDisplacementMap` through the ordinary `filter` property, on the element's own rendering. So glass over `UI/Theme/Wallpaper.swift`-equivalent content is reproducible in kind; glass over the desktop is not.

WORSE: the two halves are mutually exclusive in this stack. There is an open, never-worked WebView2 bug (WebView2Feedback #4945, filed 2024-11-23, still open) in which `backdrop-filter: blur` fails once the controller's `DefaultBackgroundColor` alpha is 0, which is precisely what wry sets for a transparent window (`src/webview2/mod.rs:127` and `:467`, `set_background_color(controller, (0,0,0,0))`). Wails hit the same wall (wails #2340). So the configuration needed for any desktop show-through is the configuration that breaks the in-page filter path.

NO ESCAPE HATCH INSIDE TAURI. To feed real desktop pixels to a shader you would need Windows.Graphics.Capture in Rust plus your own D3D/DComp visual composited under the web content. wry creates the webview with `CreateCoreWebView2Controller(hwnd, ...)` / `CreateCoreWebView2ControllerWithOptions(hwnd, ...)` (mod.rs:423, :425) and never `CreateCoreWebView2CompositionController`, so there is no `RootVisualTarget` and no visual tree to compose into without forking wry. And even with a fork: suppressing the capture indicator needs `GraphicsCaptureSession.IsBorderRequired = false`, which requires a packaged app declaring the `graphicsCaptureWithoutBorder` capability plus a user consent prompt via `GraphicsCaptureAccess.RequestAccessAsync(Borderless)`; self-capture feedback needs `SetWindowDisplayAffinity(WDA_EXCLUDEFROMCAPTURE)`, which also makes the app invisible to the user's own screenshots and screen shares; and the DOM content sitting between the desktop and the glass still cannot be handed to a shader, because the web platform has no DOM-to-texture API. A permanent full-screen capture running behind a chat app on an integrated Radeon is not a parity implementation, it is a different product.

verdicts.stack: Flutter 3.47.2 stable (Dart 3.13, Impeller/Vulkan Windows embedder, native Win32 runner)
verdicts.verdict: DISQUALIFIED - Flutter can author the Liquid Glass material in full (blur + lensing + specular edge + per-frame pointer deformation) but only over content Flutter itself paints; there is no API by which a Flutter window obtains the DESKTOP behind it as a texture, and window-level transparency on Windows has been an open, unimplemented request since 2020, while the app's own source sets `window.isOpaque = false` and applies a window-sized `glassEffect` over a `.clear` fill, making the desktop the backdrop.
verdicts.glass:
Split answer, and the split is the disqualifier.

WHAT FLUTTER CAN DO (over app-drawn content): fully. `ui.ImageFilter.shader(FragmentShader)` creates an image filter from a custom GLSL fragment shader and is accepted by `BackdropFilter(filter: ...)`. The engine automatically binds `sampler2D` index 0 to the filter input (the already-rasterised content beneath) and floats 0-1 to its width/height, so the shader can sample the backdrop at arbitrary offset UVs. That is exactly the primitive needed for lensing/refraction, per-channel UV offset for chromatic fringing, and a specular edge term computed from a signed-distance field of the shape. It is a genuine shader over a genuine backdrop sample, not a blur-and-tint. This constructor is Impeller-only and throws `UnsupportedError` on other backends, and Impeller became the DEFAULT renderer on Windows (Vulkan) in Flutter 3.47, so on current stable the API is live on Windows. Pointer tracking for `.interactive()` is trivial: a `MouseRegion` writes `shader.setFloat(i, x/y)` each frame and the shader is re-rendered; no API gap.

WHAT FLUTTER CANNOT DO (over the desktop): nothing available.
- `BackdropFilter` is documented as applying "a filter to the existing painted content" bounded by the ancestor clip. "Existing painted content" is the Flutter layer tree. There is no path by which DWM-composited desktop pixels enter that tree.
- The Flutter VIEW cannot be made transparent on Windows. flutter/flutter#71735 ("Transparent Backgrounds for Flutter Windows Desktop Applications", opened 2020-12-04) is still OPEN today, 12 comments, never implemented. Flutter's desktop lead scoped it explicitly (2022-01-23): "Flutter doesn't currently control the window in any way, so making the application transparent is out of scope... This is tracking being able to make the Flutter view transparent (which is necessary for making the whole application transparent)." The only community route is the `DwmExtendFrameIntoClientArea(hwnd, MARGINS{-1})` hack in `win32_window.cpp`, or `flutter_acrylic`, which calls `DwmSetWindowAttribute` on Windows 11 >= 22523 for Acrylic/Mica/Tabbed. Those produce a DWM system effect composited BENEATH the window. The app never sees those pixels; they cannot be fed to a shader, cannot be lensed, cannot be edge-refracted. That is blur-and-tint, and it is not even blur-and-tint inside Flutter - it is blur-and-tint underneath Flutter.
- Impeller's move to Vulkan on Windows in 3.47 makes the transparency hack worse, not better: the DWM alpha route depended on the ANGLE/D3D swapchain preserving premultiplied alpha, and Win32 Vulkan surfaces conventionally expose only `VK_COMPOSITE_ALPHA_OPAQUE_BIT_KHR`. This is the single most important unverified point (probe P1).

THE ONLY ESCAPE HATCH, and why it is not a fix: a C++ plugin captures the monitor with `Windows.Graphics.Capture`, excludes the app's own HWND with `SetWindowDisplayAffinity(hwnd, WDA_EXCLUDEFROMCAPTURE)`, and hands each frame to Flutter as a D3D11 shared-handle external texture (`kFlutterDesktopGpuSurfaceTypeD3d11Texture2D`, `flutter::ExternalTextureD3d`) painted at the bottom of the scene, where `BackdropFilter(ImageFilter.shader(...))` can then sample it. Every link exists, and three of them bite: (a) DXGI shared-handle external textures crashed in `flutter_windows.dll` under Impeller on 3.47.0 (flutter/flutter#191468, filed 2026-08-21); the fix landed on `main` via PR #191017 and was confirmed 2026-09-03, but is NOT in 3.47.2 stable; (b) because the window still cannot be transparent, you are not showing the desktop, you are PAINTING a copy of it, so it is at least one frame stale and will visibly lag and shear during window drags and behind any moving content; (c) `WDA_EXCLUDEFROMCAPTURE` removes the window from every capture pipeline at the display-subsystem level, so the app becomes invisible in the owner's own screenshots and screen shares - an unacceptable side effect for a coding tool.

Net: over the app's own `Wallpaper.swift` layer and over chat content, Flutter renders the material at full fidelity and is one of the few non-Apple stacks that can. Over the desktop - which `WindowChrome.swift:116-117` (`isOpaque = false`, `backgroundColor = .clear`) and `Chrome.swift`'s `WindowBackdrop` (`shape.fill(.clear).glassEffect(in: shape)` plus a user-facing transparency slider) make the app's BASE surface, not an accent - Flutter cannot.

verdicts.stack: WPF (.NET 10 / windowsdesktop, MILCore Direct3D 9 rendering) with ShaderEffect + D3DImage/HwndHost interop, DWM system backdrop, optional Windows.UI.Composition island
verdicts.verdict: DISQUALIFIED - WPF has no API that hands the application the pixels behind its own window, and the only Windows API that does hand back a backdrop (Compositor.CreateHostBackdropBrush) is documented as un-readable and cannot run a custom shader, so the material reduces to blur-and-tint, which OD-0003 rules out.
verdicts.glass: Blur and tint only, no lensing, no specular edge, no pointer deformation. Three paths exist and all three fail. (a) DWM system backdrop: DwmSetWindowAttribute(hwnd, DWMWA_SYSTEMBACKDROP_TYPE=38, DWMSBT_TRANSIENTWINDOW) gives Desktop Acrylic behind the whole window bounds; it is system-drawn, one material per window, not per-shape (22 glass sites), has no shader hook, no specular edge and no pointer response. .NET 9/10 WPF's Fluent theme uses exactly this (DWMSBT_MAINWINDOW) and dotnet/wpf#8545 shows WPF still ships no managed API to select the type. (b) Composition host backdrop in an island: Compositor.CreateHostBackdropBrush() is the only API that samples "the area behind the visual, before the window is drawn", and its own Remarks say "The app cannot read the pixel data back", and its transparency "is a property the user can control from Settings or by using power policies". Worse, custom shaders cannot be put over it: PixelShaderEffect is marked [NoComposition] in Win2D and CompositionEffectFactory compiles only from a fixed set of built-in effects, so the graph is limited to Gaussian blur, color matrix, blend and similar. Even that island is a child HWND, and in WPF a child HWND is an HwndHost, which is subject to airspace ("each pixel belongs to exactly one technology"), always draws on top of WPF content, cannot be alpha-blended or clipped to a rounded glass shape by WPF, and is documented as not displayable at all in a Window with AllowsTransparency=true. (c) Do it by hand: Windows.Graphics.Capture (IGraphicsCaptureItemInterop::CreateForMonitor + Direct3D11CaptureFramePool.CreateFreeThreaded) genuinely can deliver desktop content as a D3D11 texture, over which a Shader Model 5 lensing/chromatic-fringe shader is trivial. But that is a screen-capture loop, not a compositor backdrop: one frame of latency, misalignment during window drag, your own window must be removed with SetWindowDisplayAffinity(WDA_EXCLUDEFROMCAPTURE) to avoid feedback (which then makes the whole app invisible to the user's own screenshots and screen sharing), and to show it under WPF content you need D3DImage, which takes a Direct3D 9 surface, so the D3D11 texture must be shared into D3D9Ex, and D3DImage "does not display Direct3D content when WPF renders in software" - which is what AllowsTransparency, RDP and front-buffer loss give you. Separately, WPF's own ShaderEffect cannot rescue the app-drawn half of the problem at fidelity: it is limited to Pixel Shader 2.0/3.0 compiled with fxc, max 4 samplers (8 with PS 3.0), 224 float constants, "if a valid PS 3.0 shader is loaded on a computer that does not have hardware support for PS 3.0, the shader is ignored" with no exception thrown, "PS 3.0 shaders do not run during software rendering", and on a multi-GPU machine "the behavior is defined by the least capable video card" - which is exactly this machine's Radeon + Parsec virtual adapter situation. And ShaderEffect samples only the element it is applied to; WPF exposes no per-frame handle to its own render target (RenderTargetBitmap is a synchronous re-render, not a 60 Hz backdrop source), so lensing the live transcript and the app-drawn Wallpaper layer behind a panel is not a sampling operation you can express either.

glass_mechanisms: WinUI 3 / Windows App SDK 2.0 (C#/.NET 10, WinRT, Microsoft.UI.Composition, Win2D + ComputeSharp.D2D1): Desktop backdrop: Microsoft.UI.Xaml.Window.SystemBackdrop = DesktopAcrylicBackdrop / MicaBackdrop, or Microsoft.UI.Composition.SystemBackdrops.DesktopAcrylicController / MicaController driven by SystemBackdropConfiguration against ICompositionSupportsSystemBackdrop; SystemBackdropElement (WinAppSDK 2.0) for a bounded region. Tunable surface is exactly {TintColor, TintOpacity, LuminosityOpacity, FallbackColor, Kind}. In-app backdrop: Microsoft.UI.Composition.Compositor.CreateBackdropBrush() feeding Compositor.CreateEffectFactory(IGraphicsEffect) -> CompositionEffectBrush on a SpriteVisual, or Microsoft.UI.Xaml.Media.AcrylicBrush / XamlCompositionBrushBase; effect vocabulary limited to the 14 composition-supported Win2D effect types. Custom shaders: Microsoft.Graphics.Canvas.Effects.PixelShaderEffect (HLSL compiled to ps_4_0_level_9_3 bytecode) or ComputeSharp.D2D1.WinUI PixelShaderEffect<T> with [D2DShaderProfile(D2D1ShaderProfile.PixelShader40)] and [D2DRequiresScenePosition], with Source1Mapping = SamplerCoordinateMapping.Offset and MaxSamplerOffset for warp/lensing, drawn through Win2D CanvasControl / CanvasAnimatedControl / CanvasVirtualImageSource or a SwapChainPanel. The two families do not interoperate: PixelShaderEffect is [NoComposition], and microsoft-ui-xaml#5025 further reports that CompositionBackdropBrush cannot sample over a SwapChainPanel, so even placing shader output under a backdrop-brushed surface does not close the loop.

Native Win32 + Direct3D 11/12 + Direct2D + DirectComposition (C++), with DirectWrite for text, HLSL for the material shaders, Windows.Graphics.Capture for desktop backdrop sampling, and ConPTY for the terminal.: Two-path material. Path A (glass over app-drawn content, e.g. over UI/Theme/Wallpaper.swift's layer): render app content to an offscreen ID3D11Texture2D, bind as SRV, run the glass HLSL (blur pyramid + SDF rim specular + refraction remap + tint), composite. No OS involvement, full fidelity. Path B (glass over the desktop): IGraphicsCaptureItemInterop::CreateForMonitor (windows.graphics.capture.interop.h) -> GraphicsCaptureItem -> Direct3D11CaptureFramePool::Create(device, DXGI_FORMAT_B8G8R8A8_UNORM or R16G16B16A16_FLOAT on HDR, bufferCount, item.Size) -> CreateCaptureSession -> StartCapture -> FrameArrived -> Direct3D11CaptureFrame::Surface as ID3D11Texture2D; SetWindowDisplayAffinity(hwnd, WDA_EXCLUDEFROMCAPTURE) to break the feedback loop; GraphicsCaptureAccess::RequestAccessAsync(Borderless) + IsBorderRequired=false to suppress the monitor-wide recording border. Both paths output into a DXGI composition swap chain (IDXGIFactory2::CreateSwapChainForComposition, DXGI_SWAP_EFFECT_FLIP_SEQUENTIAL, DXGI_SCALING_STRETCH, DXGI_ALPHA_MODE_PREMULTIPLIED) set as IDCompositionVisual::SetContent on an IDCompositionTarget for a WS_EX_NOREDIRECTIONBITMAP HWND. Pointer position for .interactive() is a per-frame cbuffer value from WM_MOUSEMOVE. Genie.metal transliterates to an HLSL pixel shader as a float2 sample-coordinate remap. Explicitly NOT used, because they cannot do lensing: DwmSetWindowAttribute(DWMWA_SYSTEMBACKDROP_TYPE) (fixed five-value enum, no parameters) and Compositor::CreateHostBackdropBrush ("The app cannot read the pixel data back").

Avalonia UI 12.1.2 (current stable, Sept 2026) on .NET 10, rendering through SkiaSharp 4.152.x / Skia, with HarfBuzzSharp shaping, the Avalonia composition renderer, and Win32/WinRT interop via Win32Properties and MicroCom.: Two disjoint mechanisms, and they cannot be combined on the same pixels.

System path (desktop backdrop, no shader): `Window.TransparencyLevelHint = WindowTransparencyLevel.AcrylicBlur` -> `Avalonia.Win32.WindowImpl.SetTransparencyAcrylicBlur()` -> `DwmSetWindowAttribute(DWMWA_USE_HOSTBACKDROPBRUSH)` + `WinUiCompositionUtils.CreateAcrylicBlurBackdropBrush(compositor)` -> `ICompositor3::CreateHostBackdropBrush()` wrapped in `WinUIGaussianBlurEffect` + `SaturationEffect` via `Compositor.CreateEffectFactory` -> `CompositionEffectBrush` on a `SpriteVisual` beneath Avalonia's surface visual in the DComp tree. Effect vocabulary is the six documented types. Pixels unreadable by the app. Mica is the same shape via `ICompositorWithBlurredWallpaperBackdropBrush::TryCreateBlurredWallpaperBackdropBrush` plus Blend 22/23. Note also that `WindowTransparencyLevel` is documented as a HINT with a fallback chain, and the host backdrop's transparency is "a property the user can control from Settings or by using power policies" - so the look is not fully under the app's control, which is itself an OD-0003 problem.

Shader path (app-drawn backdrop, full material): `CompositionCustomVisual` + `CompositionCustomVisualHandler.OnRender(ImmediateDrawingContext ctx)` -> `ctx.TryGetFeature<ISkiaSharpApiLeaseFeature>()` -> `feature.Lease()` -> `lease.SkSurface.Snapshot(bounds)` for the backdrop `SKImage`, `lease.GrContext` for an offscreen `SKSurface.Create(grContext, true, info)` where needed -> `SKRuntimeEffect.Create(sksl, out err)`, `SKRuntimeEffectUniforms` (pointer xy, shape rect, corner radius, tint, time), `SKRuntimeEffectChildren` bound to the snapshot -> `effect.ToShader(...)` -> `canvas.DrawRect(paint)` clipped to the glass shape. Per-frame drive via `RegisterForNextAnimationFrameUpdate()` / `OnAnimationFrameUpdate()` with `CompositionNow`. `GlassEffectContainer` (spacings 2, 2, 8) maps to one snapshot shared by all glass sites in the container, rather than one snapshot per site.

Genie shader: `UI/Common/Genie.metal` is a `[[stitchable]] float2 genie(float2 position, float progress, float4 source, float2 target)` position-mapping distortion using only `clamp`, `smoothstep`, `mix`, `min`, `max` and a sentinel return. Every one of those exists in SkSL, and a coordinate-remapping shader that samples a child image is the canonical SKSL runtime-shader form. SwiftUI's `.distortionEffect(maxSampleOffset:)` offscreen pass maps to snapshotting the row subtree to an `SKImage` padded by the computed `reach`. This is a near-mechanical translation and is the LOW-risk part of the graphics work.

Qt 6.11 (current shipping release; docs served as 6.11.1/6.11.2), C++ with QML/Qt Quick on the RHI scene graph, Direct3D 11 backend on Windows, plus direct Win32/DXGI calls for anything Qt does not wrap.: Backdrop acquisition (Win32, not Qt): IDXGIOutput5::DuplicateOutput1 / IDXGIOutputDuplication::AcquireNextFrame -> IDXGIResource -> QueryInterface to ID3D11Texture2D (B8G8R8A8_UNORM, whole output, dirty/move rects available), on the same adapter Qt's RHI is using; SetWindowDisplayAffinity(hwnd, WDA_EXCLUDEFROMCAPTURE) on the app's own top-level windows to break the feedback loop. Alternative: winrt::get_activation_factory<GraphicsCaptureItem, IGraphicsCaptureItemInterop>()->CreateForMonitor(HMONITOR, ...) + Direct3D11CaptureFramePool::Create + GraphicsCaptureSession::StartCapture, but IsBorderRequired=false needs GraphicsCaptureAccess.RequestAccessAsync(Borderless) plus the graphicsCaptureWithoutBorder restricted capability in a package manifest.

Bridge into Qt: QQuickWindow::rendererInterface() / QSGRendererInterface::getResource(window, QSGRendererInterface::DeviceResource) to obtain Qt's ID3D11Device, then QNativeInterface::QSGD3D11Texture::fromNative(texture, window, size, options) on the scene-graph render thread to wrap the captured texture as a QSGTexture without copying or owning it (this is the documented replacement for the removed QQuickWindow::createTextureFromId()). If the capture device differs from Qt's device, share via IDXGIResource1::CreateSharedHandle and ID3D11Device1::OpenSharedResource1.

Material: qt6_add_shaders() runs qsb to bake GLSL 440 into SPIR-V/HLSL/.qsb; a ShaderEffect (or a QSGMaterialShader + custom QSGNode for finer control) samples the cropped window-rect subregion of that texture plus a shape mask, does the blur pass, per-channel refraction offsets for chromatic fringing, a specular term from the signed distance to the shape edge, and adaptive tint. Pointer deformation is a vec2 uniform driven by a HoverHandler, updated per frame.

Window plumbing: QQuickWindow::setDefaultAlphaBuffer(true) (or alphaBufferSize) makes the D3D11 RHI backend create a composition swapchain and go through DirectComposition, which is required because the mandatory flip-model swapchain cannot do per-pixel transparency; Qt::FramelessWindowHint plus QWindow::startSystemMove()/startSystemResize() and a QAbstractNativeEventFilter for WM_NCCALCSIZE/WM_NCHITTEST gives the app-drawn caption buttons and keeps Aero Snap.

Electron 44.x (Chromium + Node), TypeScript, with node-pty/xterm.js, electron-builder NSIS + electron-updater: Two layers, deliberately different.

Window-level surface (WindowBackdrop, the one that sits over the desktop): desktopCapturer.getSources({types:['screen']}) + ses.setDisplayMediaRequestHandler granting the screen source programmatically -> navigator.mediaDevices.getDisplayMedia -> MediaStreamTrack -> gl.texImage2D(video) each frame into a WebGL2 (or WebGPU) canvas at the bottom of the stacking context; a fragment shader crops the capture to the window's screen rect (win.getBounds + screen.getDisplayNearestPoint for DPI), then applies SDF edge refraction, multi-tap blur, specular rim, adaptive tint and a pointer-position uniform for .interactive(). win.setContentProtection(true) (SetWindowDisplayAffinity / WDA_EXCLUDEFROMCAPTURE) removes our own window from the capture to break the feedback loop. Window is opaque, so none of the documented transparent-window limitations apply.

In-window surfaces (the other 21 glassEffect sites): CSS backdrop-filter: url(#lensN) blur(Npx) saturate(...) where #lensN is an SVG <filter> containing feImage (a precomputed per-shape displacement/normal map, NOT feTurbulence, which recomputes per frame) + feDisplacementMap; the specular edge is an inset box-shadow / border-image drawn by the element itself; .interactive() sites rewrite the feDisplacementMap scale and the feImage map origin on pointermove. Because the captured desktop is now ordinary DOM content at the bottom of the document, these inner surfaces compose over it exactly as they do over app content on macOS, and the Backdrop Root restriction stops being a problem.

Genie.metal: direct transliteration to a WebGL2/WebGPU fragment shader; SwiftUI .distortionEffect maps to a full-screen quad pass over the element's rendered texture.

Rejected: win.setBackgroundMaterial('mica'|'acrylic'|'tabbed') (DWM_SYSTEMBACKDROP_TYPE) - DWM-drawn, unreadable, unshaderable, fixed recipe, and flattens to a solid colour on deactivate/battery-saver/transparency-off.

Tauri 2 (Rust core + wry/WebView2 on Windows), with window-vibrancy 0.8 for window effects: Desktop backdrop: only `window_vibrancy::apply_acrylic/apply_mica/apply_blur` (crate 0.8.0) -> `user32!SetWindowCompositionAttribute(ACCENT_ENABLE_ACRYLICBLURBEHIND | ACCENT_ENABLE_BLURBEHIND)` and `dwmapi!DwmSetWindowAttribute(DWMWA_SYSTEMBACKDROP_TYPE, DWMSBT_*)`, surfaced through Tauri as `WebviewWindowBuilder::effects()` / `WindowEffect::{Mica, Acrylic, Blur, Tabbed}` (effects require `transparent(true)`). Fixed system materials, tint colour only. In-page backdrop: CSS `backdrop-filter: url(#f)` with `feDisplacementMap` + `feBlend` (Chromium-only, samples Backdrop Root = document content only); element-local distortion (the Genie analogue) via `filter: url(#genie)` with `feDisplacementMap`; pointer response by mutating filter params on `pointermove`. Desktop pixels as a texture would require `Windows.Graphics.Capture` + `ICoreWebView2CompositionController.RootVisualTarget` with a DirectComposition visual tree, which wry does not use and does not expose.

Flutter 3.47.2 stable (Dart 3.13, Impeller/Vulkan Windows embedder, native Win32 runner): Authoring path: `.frag` GLSL (versions 460 down to 100, `sampler2D` only, no UBO/SSBO, no bools/uints, two-arg `texture()`) declared under `flutter: shaders:` in pubspec, AOT-compiled by the Flutter CLI into a backend-specific blob, loaded with `FragmentProgram.fromAsset()` -> `program.fragmentShader()`. Applied with `BackdropFilter(filter: ui.ImageFilter.shader(shader), child: ...)` inside a `ClipRRect`/`ClipPath` matching each glass shape (Circle, Capsule, rect cornerRadius 20/26 continuous, plus the `GlassEffectContainer` spacings 2/2/8). Engine auto-binds sampler 0 = filter input and floats 0-1 = input size; the app sets pointer position, tint, corner radius, IOR and edge width as further float uniforms. `ImageFilter.isShaderFilterSupported` is the runtime capability gate. Backdrop obtained: the Flutter layer tree only. Desktop backdrop obtained: NOT OBTAINABLE via any Flutter API; would require a `Windows.Graphics.Capture` plugin + `SetWindowDisplayAffinity(WDA_EXCLUDEFROMCAPTURE)` + `FlutterDesktopGpuSurfaceDescriptor` / `ExternalTextureD3d` external texture painted below the filter. Genie: `Genie.metal` is a `[[stitchable]] float2 genie(...)` coordinate-remap that returns the SOURCE coordinate per destination pixel; Flutter has no `.distortionEffect`, but the same maths becomes a one-line-longer GLSL shader that does `texture(u_src, remap(uv))`, used via `ImageFilter.shader` or `package:flutter_shaders` `AnimatedSampler`. Its `return nothing` sentinel (-100000,-100000) relies on out-of-bounds sampling returning transparent; Flutter documents `TileMode.clamp` as the default for out-of-range sampling, so the sentinel must be replaced with an explicit alpha=0 discard.

WPF (.NET 10 / windowsdesktop, MILCore Direct3D 9 rendering) with ShaderEffect + D3DImage/HwndHost interop, DWM system backdrop, optional Windows.UI.Composition island: DwmSetWindowAttribute(DWMWA_SYSTEMBACKDROP_TYPE, DWM_SYSTEMBACKDROP_TYPE.DWMSBT_TRANSIENTWINDOW/DWMSBT_MAINWINDOW) for a system-drawn window-wide Acrylic/Mica; Windows.UI.Composition Compositor.CreateHostBackdropBrush() + CompositionEffectBrush/CompositionEffectFactory (built-in effects only, pixels not readable) hosted in a DesktopWindowTarget child HWND via HwndHost; System.Windows.Media.Effects.ShaderEffect + PixelShader (ps_2_0/ps_3_0 .ps bytecode from fxc.exe) for effects over app-drawn WPF content only; System.Windows.Interop.D3DImage (SetBackBuffer with an IDirect3DSurface9/D3D9Ex shared surface, Lock/AddDirtyRect/Unlock) as the only way to get a hand-authored D3D texture into WPF's visual tree with alpha; Windows.Graphics.Capture + SetWindowDisplayAffinity(WDA_EXCLUDEFROMCAPTURE) as the only way to obtain desktop pixels at all.
